Sad
SAD
adj.
From Saxon saed, sated, full, heavy — the older sense being weighty or grave rather than merely sorrowful. Webster 1828: sorrowful; heavy; serious; grave; and, in an older use, firm or solid. Scripture uses it chiefly of the countenance, where grief becomes visible.

Biblical Definition

Sad in the Authorized Version almost always attaches to a face, because Scripture treats grief as something that shows. Joseph, himself a prisoner, notices it in two fellow prisoners and asks about it: And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6) — a man in a dungeon paying attention to other men’s faces, which is how the whole chain of his deliverance begins. Hannah’s sadness lifts before her circumstances change: after Eli blesses her, the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:18). She has not yet conceived; she has been heard. Nehemiah’s sadness in the presence of a Persian king was dangerous, and he says so: Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid (Nehemiah 2:2). And the word records two failures to receive Christ: the rich young man, he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions (Mark 10:22), and the two on the Emmaus road, whom the risen Lord found sad because they had not yet understood that the Christ must suffer (Luke 24:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SAD as sorrowful; affected with grief; heavy in spirit; also serious, grave, or not light; and in an older and now rare sense, firm, solid, or heavy in substance.

expand to see more

SAD, a. — Sorrowful; affected with grief; cast down in spirits.

Serious; grave; not light or volatile; as, a sad and weighty matter.

Causing sorrow; calamitous; as, a sad accident, or a sad reverse.

In an old and rare sense, heavy, firm, or close in texture; as, sad bread — the root meaning of full or sated.

From Saxon saed, sated, heavy — connected with satiate and with the Latin satis, enough.

Key Scripture

Genesis 40:6 — "And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad."

1 Samuel 1:18 — "And she said, Let thine handmaid find grace in thy sight. So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad."

Nehemiah 2:2 — "Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid,"

Mark 10:22 — "And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions."

Luke 24:17 — "And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad?"

Modern Corruption

Mark 10:22 records the only person in the Gospels who came to Christ eagerly and went away sad, and the modern habit of presenting the gospel as an addition to a life rather than a claim upon it has removed the possibility of that outcome.

expand to see more

The young man ran to Christ, knelt, and asked the right question, and Mark says the Lord beholding him loved him before naming the one thing he lacked. The demand was total and particular: sell what thou hast, give to the poor, come and follow. He went away sad, and the Lord let him go without softening the terms or calling after him with a smaller offer. Modern evangelism is largely constructed to prevent this scene. The claim is presented as an addition to the hearer’s existing life, the cost is postponed to a later stage of discipleship, and no one is ever permitted to leave sorrowful. But a gospel that cannot produce Mark 10:22 is not the gospel Christ preached, and the church that never sees anyone walk away is probably not asking anyone for anything.

The other three uses supply the balance, and it is a real one. Hannah’s countenance was no more sad before her circumstances changed at all — sorrow lifted by being heard, which is what prayer often accomplishes and what it always accomplishes eventually. Joseph, in prison, looked at two men’s faces and asked why they were sad, and God used the question. And the risen Christ walked seven miles with two sad disciples and began not with comfort but with a rebuke and an exposition: O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken… And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. Their sadness was cured by Scripture opened, and their hearts burned before they knew who He was.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, and of the countenance, sad or downcast; zaaph (H2196), to be sad, to rage; Greek stugnazo (G4768), to become gloomy, to lower as a sky; skuthropos (G4659), of a sad countenance.

expand to see more

Hebrew zaaph (H2196) — to be out of humour, sad, vexed; behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6).

Hebrew panim ra — literally an evil face; the idiom for a downcast countenance in Nehemiah 2:2.

Greek stugnazo (G4768) — to become gloomy, as a darkening sky; he was sad at that saying (Mark 10:22).

Greek skuthropos (G4659) — of a gloomy countenance; the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:17), and the hypocrites of Matthew 6:16.

Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorrowful; the New Testament’s general verb of sorrow.

Usage

"Behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6) — a prisoner noticing other prisoners’ faces."

"Her countenance was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:18) — sorrow lifted before circumstances changed."

"He was sad at that saying, and went away grieved (Mark 10:22) — the one man who came running and left sorrowful."
